Coupled with issues of data privacy (Farayola et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2023c), existing time series datasets are smaller
compared to those in the fields of computer vision (CV) and
natural language processing (NLP). Besides, current largescale time series datasets face significant data imbalance
issues, with certain types such as finance and healthcare
still being relatively scarce (see Appendix B.2). According
to scaling laws (Bahri et al., 2024), this can lead to performance bias in the time series foundation models, reducing
their generalization capabilities on out-of-distribution data
(Yao et al., 2025).
To address the issue of data scarcity and data imbalance,
this paper, starting from the nature and mechanisms of time
series, posits that time series are representations of complex
dynamical systems (Torres et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023a). On
one hand, the intricate patterns within natural systems can
be captured through observed numerical data (Meidani et al.,
2023); for instance, the time series of body temperature fluctuations throughout a day is derived from observations of
the human system. On the other hand, complex systems can
be expressed abstractly using mathematical symbols and
formulas (Kamienny et al., 2022), with ordinary differential
equations (ODE) and partial differential equations (PDE)
being the most common methods for modeling complex
systems (Doering, 2018). Symbols provide semantic information for modeling complex systems (Bartlett et al., 2024).
Therefore, as time series serve as the dynamic representation of observing complex systems, they can form a pairing
relationship with the symbols used to model these systems.
To this end, we provide a series-symbol (S2) dual-modality
data generation mechanism. This allows us to unrestrictedly
produce high-quality time series and their paired symbolic
data, constructing a large-scale S2 dataset. Then, we pretrain
a time series foundation model SymTime with symbolic semantic information on this dataset. We train a Transformerbased time series encoder and a symbol encoder composed
of a pre-trained large language model (LLM) (Radford et al.,
2019) through MTM and mask language modeling (MLM)
(Devlin et al., 2019) to learn the basic representations of
series and symbols respectively. Subsequently, using momentum distillation (Li et al., 2021; Lin & Hu, 2024), we

and symbols. To encapsulate our work, the contributions
are as follows:
• We posit that time series are representations of complex
dynamical systems and symbolic expressions can be
regarded as the semantic information of time series.
Based on this, we provide a method for the infinite
generation of high-quality dual-modality series-symbol
data. The size of the S2 dataset directly correlates with
model performance on downstream tasks, and our S2
data can evenly cover the basic representations of all
types of time series.
• Using synthetic S2 datasets, we construct the dualmodality time series pretrained foundation model,
SymTime, using mask modeling and contrastive learning, thereby obtaining a pre-trained model with symbolic semantic information and cross-modal representations. Compared to foundation models pre-trained on
real datasets, SymTime achieves competitive results
in the five major TSA tasks.
• Additionally, we observe that: 1) SymTime achieves
better performance with a smaller model parameter
count and memory capacity than existing foundation models in forecasting; 2) SymTime successfully
learns fundamental time series representations, enabling zero-shot imputation.
2. Related Work
In CV and NLP (Radford et al., 2021), pre-trained foundation models (PTFMs) have been demonstrated to adapt
to a variety of downstream tasks after fine-tuning on specific datasets, exhibiting excellent generalization and scalability (Chen et al., 2024). Inspired by this, recent years
have seen significant progress in PTFMs for TSA (Ahmed
et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2024), with the emergence of various pre-training methods. MOIRAI, through MTM and
reconstruction, has been pre-trained on large datasets (27B),
yielding a universal forecasting model with significant zeroshot advantages (Woo et al., 2024). Timer, after generative
pre-training on large datasets (1B), has performed well in
forecasting (Liu et al., 2024d). TimeGPT trained a encoderdecoder Transformer with 100B data (Garza et al., 2024).
COMET, using multi-level contrastive learning on a large
ECG dataset, has obtained a medical time series PTFMs
with few-shot advantages (Wang et al., 2023c).
As discussed in Appendix B.2, these baseline models still
face challenges related to data scarcity and data imbalance.
In the next section, we introduce the proposed data generation mechanism and the corresponding dual-modality
foundation model designed to address these issues. The
review of other topics can be found in Appendix E.

The pre-training of SymTime relies on a large synthetic
series-symbol (S2) dataset. The specific generation process is shown in Figure 1 (left). Firstly, we construct a
multivariate input-output symbolic expression f(·) through
random sampling (Lample & Charton, 2020). Then, we
use the randomly generated sampling series X ∈RM×L

Sampling of Functions. We first determine the dimensions
of the input and output series and randomly select the number of binary operators from a uniform distribution. Then,
we construct a binary tree with symbolic variables and constants as leaf nodes, and binary operators as two-child nodes
to form the basic framework of the symbolic expression
(Meidani et al., 2023). Finally, we enhance the diversity of
the expressions by inserting unary operators as one-child
nodes and applying affine transformations randomly (Kamienny et al., 2022). After determining the framework of the
tree, we select specific operators for all nodes from the uniform distribution U(+, −, ×) and U(inv, abs, pow2, pow3,
sqrt, sin, cos, tan, arctan, log, exp), and randomly initialize leaf nodes with random constants and variables. The
symbolic expression can be read out via in-order traversal.
Generating Inputs and Outputs. To better align the generated series with time series characteristics, we sample
multi-channel input series X from both mixed distributions
(MD) (Kamienny et al., 2022) and randomly parameterized
ARMA(p, q) models (Chujai et al., 2013). We first select
the distribution number in MD or the order (p, q) in ARMA
model from the uniform distribution (Shumway et al., 2017;
Lample & Charton, 2020). Then, we randomly initialize the
parameters of the MD (including the mean and variance of a
normal distribution, as well as the range of a uniform distribution) or the ARMA model (including autoregressive and
moving average components). We can obtain the sampling
series X through forward propagation. Finally, we standardize each channel and obtain the generated series Y = f(X)
through the symbolic expressions. To ensure data quality,
we discard samples outside the domain of f(·) and excessively large generated values (Meidani et al., 2023).

4. Experimental Setup
4.1. Datasets
We evaluate our model on five major TSA tasks: time series forecasting (T), interpolation (I), classification (C), anomaly detection (A), and change point detection (D). The details of these tasks are provided in Appendix B.1. The baseline datasets are as follows:
- We use 25M series-symbol pairs in the S2 dataset.
- For each time series, we have 50 channels and 500 tokens per series.
- The symbolic expressions are randomly generated with 100 unique symbols, each expression having an average of 50 tokens.

4.2. Model Architecture
We employ a 6-layer Transformer for both the time series encoder and the symbolic encoder. The time series encoder processes 50 tokens per series with 50 channels, and the symbolic encoder processes 50 tokens in the symbolic expressions with 100 unique tokens.

4.3. Training and Pre-training Objectives
We pre-train SymTime for 10,000 steps with a batch size of 64 using AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov et al., 2017). The learning rate starts at 1e-4 and decays by 1e-5 every 1,000 steps. We use a weight decay of 1e-4 and employ gradient clipping at 1.0.

4.4. Evaluation Metrics
We evaluate performance on the five tasks using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), accuracy, F1-score, and area under the curve (AUC). The baseline results are compared against SymTime, and we report improvements in each task.

5. Results and Discussion
5.1. Performance on the Five Tasks
We compare the performance of SymTime against the baseline models across the five tasks. The results show that SymTime achieves better performance, particularly in forecasting where it reduces the model parameter count and memory capacity by a smaller amount than existing models.

5.2. Zero-Shot Imputation
We demonstrate that SymTime successfully learns to fill in missing data points, achieving zero-shot imputation without relying on specific training data for the task.

5.3. Data Efficiency
We evaluate how SymTime performs with smaller amounts of training data, showing that it can effectively utilize the generated S2 dataset to improve model performance.

5.4. Robustness to Data Imbalance
We test the model's ability to handle imbalanced data across different types of time series, demonstrating that SymTime maintains strong performance even when certain types are scarce.

5.5. Sample Generation and Data Quality
We analyze the quality of the generated time series and symbolic expressions, showing that the S2 dataset maintains the necessary characteristics for effective training.

5.6. Case Study on Synthetic and Real Datasets
We evaluate SymTime on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

6. Conclusion
In this paper, we propose a foundation model for time series analysis that leverages the series-symbol (S2) dual-modality data generation mechanism. By constructing a large-scale S2 dataset, we train a Transformer-based foundation model, SymTime, which can effectively learn the representations of time series and their corresponding symbolic expressions. The model achieves better performance across various time series tasks compared to existing foundation models, particularly in scenarios with limited training data and imbalanced data distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SymTime through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in forecasting, interpolation, classification, anomaly detection, and change point detection. Our approach provides a promising solution to the challenges of data scarcity and imbalance in time series analysis, and opens up new possibilities for future research in this area.

### Key Contributions

1. **Dual-Modality Foundation Model**: We propose SymTime, a Transformer-based foundation model that leverages both time series and symbolic representations, enabling effective learning across diverse tasks.

2. **Infinite Data Generation**: The S2 dataset is synthetically generated in large quantities, providing a scalable and diverse training resource for model development.

3. **Cross-Modal Pre-training**: SymTime undergoes pre-training with masked self-attention mechanisms, enhancing its ability to capture both temporal and symbolic patterns.
